title: Tropical weather update 2026: A Pacific storm could bring rain to Texas later this week - ABC13 Houston
text:
Tropical weather update 2026: A Pacific storm could bring rain to Texas later this week - ABC13 Houston 
 24/7 Live Houston Southwest Southeast Northwest Northeast Tropical Weather 
 A Pacific storm could bring rain to Texas later this week 
 By Travis Herzog , David Tillman , Elita Loresca , Elyse Smith , Kevin Roth Tuesday, October 27, 2026 12:56PM 
 Tropical Storm Vance could help our rain chances later this week. KTRK October 27 Update
 Tropical Storm Vance has weakened slightly, with winds of 45 mph, and is moving northwest off Mexico's coast. Heavy rain could cause flooding and mudslides in parts of western Mexico through Thursday, while dangerous waves and rip currents are expected along the coast. Vance could eventually send some moisture toward Texas later this week. Tropical development is not expected in the Atlantic.
 October 26 Update
 Tropical development is not expected in the Atlantic. However, Tropical Storm Vance continues to drift off the coast of Mexico. It is expected to weaken over the next several days. Heavy rain could cause flooding and mudslides, while large waves and dangerous rip currents may threaten people along the Mexican coast. Vance could eventually send some moisture toward Texas later this week.
 October 25 Update
 The Atlantic remains quiet, but storms in the Pacific are already impacting our weather. Hurricane Vance off the southwest coast of Mexico is pushing some high clouds into Texas today, which will in turn keep the high temperatures a bit cooler than what we saw yesterday. That same moisture connection could also help bring some rain chances into the area later this week.
 October 24 Update
 The quiet stretch of weather in the Atlantic Basin continues, with no development expected over the next 7 days. In the Pacific, things remain more active. Hurricane Vance remains just off the west coast of Mexico, and could eventually send some moisture our way towards the end of this upcoming week.
 October 23 Update
 The Atlantic has gone quiet with no tropical development expected over the next seven days. However the Pacific remains active with one named storm. Vance has strenghtened to a hurricane and will continue to intensify over the weekend. There are currently no hurricane watches or warnings for coastal areas. However, large waves from the storm may reach parts of southern and southwestern Mexico this weekend. Vance could eventually send some moisture toward Texas late next week.
 October 22 Update
 Subtropical Storm Josephine has formed off the U.S. East Coast. It is expected to grow stronger and become a powerful non-tropical storm with hurricane-force winds by Friday. There are no coastal watches or warnings in effect, but strong wind gusts and some coastal flooding are possible along parts of the northeastern U.S. Large ocean waves and dangerous rip currents are also affecting parts of the East Coast and Atlantic Canada.
 Meanwhile, Tropical Storm Vance has formed in the eastern Pacific south of Mexico. It is expected to strengthen quickly and could become a major hurricane by Saturday. Large waves and dangerous rip currents may affect parts of Mexico's southern and southwestern coast this weekend into next week. Vance could eventually send some moisture toward Texas late next week.
 October 21 Update
 A powerful storm off the U.S. East Coast could develop some tropical storm features over the next day or two. Formation odds remain at 40 percent. Even if it doesn't become a tropical storm, strong winds, coastal flooding, and dangerous waves are expected along parts of the East Coast.
 Meanwhile in the Pacific, a low-pressure system spinning a few hundred miles south of southern Mexico is becoming more organized. A tropical depression is expected to form within the next day or so. It is expected to move west or west-northwest at about 10 mph and stay far from land. Formation odds remain at 90 percent.
 October 20 Update
 A strong storm off the coast of North Carolina may develop into a tropical or subtropical system as it moves northeast and farther out to sea. Parts of the East Coast could experience strong winds, coastal flooding, and dangerous waves, while the chance of the storm developing is 40 percent within 7 days. Meanwhile in the Pacific, a low-pressure system spinning a few hundred miles south of southern Mexico is becoming more organized. A tropical depression is expected to form within the next day or so. It is expected to move west or west-northwest at about 10 mph and stay far from land. Formation odds remain at 90 percent.
 October 19 Update
 In the Pacific, Tropical Storm Trudy is weakening quickly and is expected to lose its tropical storm strength by tonight. Although it is weakening, its large waves could still create dangerous surf and rip currents along parts of Mexico's coast.
 Farther south, an area of showers and thunderstorms has formed several hundred miles south of Guatemala. Conditions are favorable for this system to develop into a tropical depression around the middle of the week as it moves west or west-northwest, staying away from southern Mexico's coast. The chance of development is 90% over the next seven days.
 In the Atlantic, we're monitoring the potential for development off the southeastern U.S. coast. It could slowly gain some tropical storm features later this week as it moves northeast, but conditions may stop it from developing by the weekend. Even if it does not become a tropical storm, strong winds, coastal flooding, and dangerous waves are expected along parts of the East Coast over the next few days, no threat to residents living along the Gulf.
 October 18 Update
 The National Hurricane Center is monitoring an area of potential development off the eastern seaboard of the United States. Current development odds are at 30%, but any development is not a factor for us here in Texas regardless. The rest of the Atlantic Basin, including the Gulf, remains quiet.
 October 17 Update
 Let's start with the good news, no tropical development is expected over the next week. Along with us being on the quieter side of hurricane season, we're also now at the time of the year where cold fronts would push any potential storms in to the Eastern Gulf instead of towards Texas. That doesn't quite mean our risk of storms is zero, but it is quite low. The Pacific basin remains active, with hurricane Trudy off the coast of Mexico and another system likely to develop in the coming days. Neither will impact our weather.
 October 16 Update
 The Pacific remains active with two storms impacting portions of Mexico and Baja California. A hurricane named Trudy and a tropical storm named Simon. Originally it looked like both storms would curve into Mexico and send moisture into Texas, but it now looks like both will curve away from Mexico and avoid sending moisture into Texas next week. The Atlantic remains quiet with no development expected over the next 7 days.
 October 15 Update
 The Atlantic remains quiet with no development expected over the next 7 days. Two Pacific storms continue to impact portions of Mexico and Baja California. A hurricane named Simon and a tropical storm named Trudy. Originally it looked like both storms would curve into Mexico and send moisture into Texas, but it now looks like both will curve away from Mexico and avoid sending moisture into Texas next week.
 October 14 Update
 As the Atlantic remains quiet, we are tracking two Pacific storms, a hurricane named Simon and a tropical storm named Trudy. Hurricane Simon will bring hurricane conditions for parts of Mexico and Baja California. It will also be possible Simon sends heavy rain into West Texas and the Panhandle later this week, then next week Trudy could send rain toward our part of Texas.
 October 13 Update
 It's pretty quiet across the Atlantic basin with no activity expected in the Gulf or Caribbean. The Atlantic is pretty quiet too with only one tropical wave near the Cabo Verde Islands that has a low chance of developing over the next 7 days.
 Hurricane Simon continues to swirl offshore of western Mexico, weakening to a category one hurricane. This has been a slow-moving storm system where heavy rains and hurricane-force winds have impacted the coastline. Simon is set to track north and make landfall in northern Mexico later this week, where moisture from the remnant system could move into the Southwest and West Texas later this week.
 October 12 Update
 We'll start with what's most important to us: There's no development expected in the Gulf over at least the next 7 days. We do have one potential storm developing in the eastern Atlantic, but development odds are low (20%), and it's not moving this direction anyways. The Pacific remains very active, highlighted by Hurricane Simon hugging the coast of Mexico. An active Pacific basin and quiet Atlantic is a typical pattern in an El Nino year, and we are certainly seeing it play out that way so far in 2026.
 October 11 Update
 Rain from the remnants of Isaias is spreading through the mid-Atlantic and Northeast, but the damaging winds and flooding rains are no longer a threat. With Isaias now essentially gone, the Atlantic basin is quiet again, with only one area of low development odds in the far eastern Atlantic near Africa. The Pacific basin is much more active, including Cat 4 Hurricane Simon impacting Mexico. Some of Simon's moisture could spread our way, helping to bring back some rain chances this upcoming week.
 October 10 Update
 Isaias is now spreading across the Southeast U.S., but it's far from the powerful system it once was. Wind speeds are down to 35mph, but rain continues through Alabama, Tennessee, the Carolinas, and more. Rain from this system will continue spreading up through the east coast today and tomorrow. In its wake we are back to quiet weather across the tropics, no development is expected over the next 7 days in the Atlantic basin.
 October 9 8:30 p.m. Update
 Hurricane Isaias made landfall near Destin Florida around 8:30 p.m. on Friday.
 October 9 7 a.m. Update
 Hurricane Isaias has officially reached Cat 3 strength this morning, with sustained winds of 120mph. The storm continues moving north, and will make landfall somewhere between Pensacola, Florida and Mobile, AL later today. Along with the destructive winds, powerful storm surge, flooding rain, and numerous tornadoes are expected. While this is a high impact storm for parts of the Gulf Coast, it has only minimal impact on our weather, and the impact is largely positive. Dry air wrapping around the west side of the storm is pushing into Southeast Texas, and that will help keep the humidity at bay through the weekend.
 October 8 7 a.m. Update
 Isaias has strengthened to a hurricane with winds of 80 mph and is expected to strengthen even more before reaching the Gulf Coast. It is expected to remain a strong hurricane as it approaches the northern Gulf coast Friday night. Coastal flooding is a major concern. Storm surge could push several feet of ocean water onto normally dry land. Some areas could see 5-7 feet of water above ground. Hurricane warnings are in effect from Ocean Springs, Mississippi, to the Bay/Gulf County line in Florida.
 Besides Isaias, we are tracking a new Pacific storm named Simon. This one could eventually send moisture into Texas to boost rain chances Monday and Tuesday. Rachel is also predicted to bring flooding rains into the southwestern United States over the weekend.
 October 7 6 a.m. Update
 Tropical Storm Isaias has formed in the Bay of Campeche and is getting stronger... could become our first hurricane of the season by Thursday. No coastal watches or warnings, however hurricane watches may be issued for parts of the U.S. Gulf Coast later today. Isaias is expected to make a north turn toward the northern Gulf Coast on Thursday and Friday. Its winds are around 40 mph... rapid strengthening is expected and could become a strong hurricane before reaching the Gulf Coast on Friday. However, there is still uncertainty about exactly where it will go, so the forecast could change. Southeast Texas will stay well west of Isaias, so no direct impacts are expected. However, the system could still cause rough seas, stronger rip currents, and some minor flooding along beaches facing the Gulf.
 October 6 4 p.m. Update
 The disturbance we've been monitoring in the Bay of Campeche has become Tropical Depression Nine Tuesday afternoon with winds of 35 mph and gusts up to 45 mph. The system is slowly moving east at 5 mph and is forecast to strengthen to a tropical storm late Tuesday night. Then it would become named storm Isaias. Isaias is then forecast to quickly turn north into the central Gulf and strengthen into a category two storm before making landfall somewhere between New Orleans and Pensacola late Friday night. Areas in the storm zone could receive torrential flooding rains, hurricane-force winds and a dangerous storm surge. And with a forecast like this, Southeast Texas would see minimal impacts, if any, with no direct impacts expected at this time.
 October 6 Update
 A tropical system in the Bay of Campeche is becoming more organized and has a 90% chance of developing into a tropical depression. It could bring heavy rain and gusty winds to parts of Mexico's Yucatan Peninsula before turning north or northeast toward the northern Gulf coast later this week. It's still too early to know the exact track or impacts, but people from the Florida Panhandle to Louisiana should closely monitor the forecast. NOAA and Air Force aircraft are scheduled to collect important data on the system today and tomorrow.
 October 5 Update
 A tropical system may develop in the Bay of Campeche later this week, with a 70% chance of formation over the next 7 days. Regardless of whether it becomes a tropical system, more rain, stronger winds, and rougher seas are expected near the coast and over the Gulf.
 Hurricane Rachel remains a Category 1 hurricane but is expected to gradually weaken. Meanwhile, a large area of thunderstorms and showers is developing southwest of Mexico. Weather conditions there are favorable for the system to slowly become stronger. It could develop into a tropical depression this week as it moves slowly toward the west or northwest, staying just offshore of the southern coast of Mexico.
 October 4 Update
 Eyes back on the Gulf with a tropical disturbance attempting to take shape. The National Hurricane Center has tagged an area of deep tropical moisture in the southern Gulf with a 30% chance of tropical development over the next 7 days. There isn't great model agreement yet on this system, where it goes, or even if it forms. What we do know is that the typical pattern for storms in the Gulf in October favors storms moving into the eastern Gulf, not the western Gulf in our neck of the woods. Still, we're keeping a watchful eye on this potential system.
 October 3 8 p.m. Update
 We're monitoring the Bay of Campeche for potential tropical development next week as a tropical low could form with the help of high tropical moisture in the Central American Gyre. It's a low, 20% chance over the next 7 days and typically tropical development in the Caribbean and Gulf this time of year begins to favor an eastward trajectory towards Florida than Texas. Either way, right now we've increased rain chances to 20% Friday and Saturday of next week to account for the possibility that tropical moisture is nearby the Texas coastline. At this time it's a low chance of a tropical system making landfall in Southeast Texas.
 October 3 Update
 The record streak of quiet weather in the Atlantic continues. No tropical development is expected over the next 7 days. We;ve already broken the record for the deepest we've ever been in hurricane season without a hurricane (since the satellite era), and it looks like we'll add at least another week to that streak. Long-range models do show signs of some sort of disturbance in the southern Gulf, but October typically favors storms moving towards the eastern Gulf rather than the western Gulf.
 October 2 Update
 The Pacific remains active with two systems to track. No threat to Texas at this time. Meanwhile, the leftovers of former Tropical Storm Fay are located several hundred miles southeast of Bermuda. There are some thunderstorms, but dry air and strong winds should keep the system from getting stronger. It will move slowly north-northwest, east of Bermuda. Formation odds are low, only a 10% chance of developing into a stronger tropical system over the next 48 hours or the next 7 days. No threat to land at this time.
 October 1 Update
 The Pacific remains active with three systems to track. No threat to Texas at this time. Meanwhile, the Atlantic turns quiet to start off the new month.
 September 30 Update
 The Pacific remains active with three systems to monitor. However, remnants from Polo is the only system that could steer moisture into Texas. Rain and storm chances will increase along with the potential for flooding. Highest rainfall totals across the state will stay north or west of us, stretching from North Texas to the Hill Country, but we'll be keeping an eye on the potential for heavy rain locally in the latter portions of the work week.
 September 29 Update
 The Pacific remains active with three named storms. However, Hurricane Polo is the only system we are closely monitoring as moisture is steered into Texas. Rain and storm chances will increase along with the potential for flooding. Highest rainfall totals across the state will stay north or northwest of us, stretching from North Texas to the Hill Country, but we'll be keeping an eye on the potential for heavy rain locally in the latter portions of the work week.
 September 28 Update
 Overall, the Pacific is much more active than the Atlantic right now, with several tropical systems being monitored. Hurricane Polo is the system we are closely monitoring as moisture is steered into Texas, rain and storm chances will increase along with the potential for flooding. Highest rainfall totals across the state will stay north or northwest of us, stretching from North Texas to the Hill Country, but we'll be keeping an eye on the potential for heavy rain locally in the latter portions of the work week.
 September 27 Update
 First and foremost, the Atlantic basin, which includes the Gulf, the Caribbean, and the Atlantic Ocean remains fairly quiet. We have one named storm in the Atlantic, Fay, but it's a non-issue as it stays over water in the Eastern Atlantic Ocean. Fay is the 6th named storm in the Atlantic basin, none of which have reached hurricane strength, adding to our record hurricane drought this year.
 The Pacific is much more active, as we currently have 3 named storms, a tropical depression, and another area the NHC is monitoring for a high chance of development. Of that activity, it's Hurricane Polo that we are keeping a close watch on. The storm will cross over Mexico from the eastern Pacific and weaken, but in the process it will pump some added moisture into Texas, increasing rain chances and the potential for flooding rains across the state. Right now it looks like the highest rainfall totals across the state will stay north or northwest of us, stretching from North Texas to the Hill Country, but we'll be keeping an eye on the potential for heavy rain locally in the latter portions of the work week.
 September 26 Update
 Gonzalo continues to bring tropical storm conditions to the Cabo Verde Islands, but will begin to move away later today. Fay is still holding on but is not expected to affect any land areas.
 In the Pacific Ocean, Hurricane Polo is moving along the coast of Mexico. Later next week, Polo could send some extra moisture into Texas, which could lead to more clouds and rain there.
 Hurricane Nolo continues to strengthen as it churns south of the Hawaiian islands. Strong winds are already affecting some areas, especially higher and mountainous places, and gusty winds could affect all of the Hawaiian Islands through the weekend. It is also expected to bring very heavy rain, especially to the Big Island and Maui. Parts of eastern and southern Hawaii's Big Island could receive 8 to 12 inches of rain, with some areas getting as much as 16 inches.
 September 25 Update
 Gonzalo has formed over the eastern Atlantic Ocean, expected to bring tropical storm conditions to the Cabo Verde Islands. Fay is still holding on but is not expected to affect any land areas.
 In the Pacific Ocean, Hurricane Polo is moving along the coast of Mexico. Later next week, Polo could send some extra moisture into Texas, which could lead to more clouds and rain there. Nolo has strengthened to a hurricane and bares watching as it is expected to move toward Hawaii and could bring another round of strong winds and heavy rain. Nolo could become a major hurricane over the weekend.
 September 24 Update
 Fay has formed again over the eastern Atlantic Ocean, but the good news is that it is not expected to affect any land areas.
 In the Pacific Ocean, Hurricane Polo is moving along the coast of Mexico. Later next week, Polo could send some extra moisture into Texas, which could lead to more clouds and rain there. Tropical Storm Nolo is another storm that bares watching as it is expected to move toward Hawaii and could bring another round of strong winds and heavy rain. People in Hawaii should continue to pay attention to weather updates as the storm gets closer. Nolo is expected to strengthen and could become a major hurricane over the weekend.
 September 23 Update
 Fay has dissipated. Meanwhile, there is a region off the west coast of Africa that has a medium chance of developing over the next 7 days.
 Meanwhile, the Pacific is becoming more and more active. Hurricane Polo remains a powerful and dangerous storm as a category 4 hurricane off the west coast of Mexico. Polo is not forecast to make landfall at this time over the next 7 days but could eventually send some moisture and rain into Texas next week. There's also tropical storm Odalys and tropical depression Fifteen-E.
 September 22 Update
 Tropical Storm Fay continues to weaken Tuesday in the eastern Pacific and is forecast to become a tropical depression later today. And while the rest of the Atlantic basin remains quiet, there is a region off the west coast of Africa that has a low chance of developing over the next 7 days.
 Meanwhile, the Pacific is becoming more and more active. Hurricane Polo has rapidly intensified overnight off the west coast of Mexico. The storm becoming a category 4 hurricane Tuesday with winds of 150 mph. Polo is not forecast to make landfall at this time over the next 7 days but will continue to swirl off the west coast of Mexico, the system gradually tracking northwest later this week. There's also tropical storm Odalys and two other regions with medium to high odds of development over the next 7 days.
 September 21 Update
 Tropical Storm Fay is slowly weakening. Winds have dropped to about 65 mph, and the storm is barely moving right now. Fay is expected to continue getting weaker and could lose its tropical storm characteristics within a day or two.
 Meanwhile, two storms to monitor in the Paciifc. Tropical Storm Odalys continues moving northwest with winds around 45 mph. The storm is expected to gradually get stronger and could become a hurricane by the middle of the week. It will also make several turns, eventually moving toward the northeast by the end of the week.Tropical Storm Polo has formed and is quickly getting stronger off the coast of southwestern Mexico. Polo could become a hurricane later today and a major hurricane in a couple of days. Heavy rain could cause dangerous flooding and mudslides, while large waves could create dangerous surf and rip currents along the coast. Tropical moisture from the remnant system could then push farther north, possibly bringing heavy rains to parts of West Texas next week.
 September 20 Update
 Tropical Storm Fay formed in the eastern Atlantic early Sunday morning, becoming the sixth named storm of the Atlantic Hurricane season. The storm is expected to swirl south of the Azores over the next few days before weakening later this week in the central Atlantic. The storm does not pose any threat to land at this time.
 In the Pacific, Tropical Storm Odalys has formed with winds of 45 mph. This system is expected to strengthen to a category one hurricane though poses no threat to land at this time either. Then there are two other regions to watch for potential development to the east and west of Odalys. The tropical wave closer to western Mexico could become a hurricane and bring heavy rains to Mexico later this week. The tropical moisture from the remnant system could then push farther north, possibly bringing heavy rains to parts of West Texas next week.
 September 19 Update
 Tropical Depression Six forms in the eastern Atlantic southwest of the Azores Saturday with winds of 35 mph. The system is expected to strengthen to weak tropical storm over the weekend and would gain the name Fay if it did. This will also be a short-lived tropical system, likely weakening in the eastern Atlantic well south of the Azores next week.
 In the Pacific there are three areas to monitor for potential development over the next 7 days. One tropical wave near the west coast of Mexico has a high likelihood of becoming a tropical system and could potentially bring heavy rains to New Mexico and West Texas near the end of the month.
 September 18 Update
 There's one area to watch in the eastern Atlantic, located several hundred miles southwest of the Azores. This system has a 30% chance of developing over the next 7 days.
 The Pacific remains very active with three areas that could become tropical storms during the next 7 days. One near Baja California has an 80% chance of forming within a week. Another near Hawaii has a 40% chance, while one south of Mexico also has an 80% chance. Gradual development will be possible.
 September 16 Update
 We continue to monitor a system in the Central Atlantic located just east of Bermuda. This system has become a little more organized. The system could slowly get stronger over the next few days. It is expected to move west today and may turn south on Friday. There is about a 40% chance of development over the next 7 days. In the Pacific, two weather systems are being watched. One south of Mexico has a 70% chance of developing over the next week. Another near Baja California has a 60% chance. Both could slowly strengthen over the next several days.
 September 15 Update
 A weather system far east of Bermuda is causing scattered showers and thunderstorms. It may become a tropical depression later this week as it moves west. Formation odds have increased to 40% during the next 7 days. Meanwhile, in the Eastern Pacific, Tropical Depression Fifteen-E is moving west at about 10 mph with winds near 35 mph. It is expected to stay about the same strength for the next few days with no threat to land. Tropical Depression Norbert is moving west at about 14 mph with winds near 35 mph. It is weakening and is expected to become a leftover low-pressure system Wednesday morning.
 September 14 Update
 The Atlantic is staying quiet, with only a small chance of tropical development over the northern Atlantic through the end of the week. In the eastern Pacific, Tropical Storm Norbert is weakening as it moves west and is expected to disappear early this week. Tropical Depression Fifteen-E could become a tropical storm today, but it is also expected to weaken as it moves west. If it gets a name, it would be Odalys.
 September 13 Update
 There's a slim chance of tropical development around Bermuda, but outside of that, the Atlantic basin remains quiet. We will likely continue our record-setting stretch in the Atlantic of zero hurricanes for at least another week. The Pacific remains active, but none of the storms will have any impact on our local weather.
 September 12 Update
 High wind shear, attributable to El Nino, is keeping things quiet in the Atlantic basin. No development is expected over the next 7 days, despite us being in the peak of hurricane season currently. There have been zero hurricanes so far in the Atlantic Basin, which breaks the all time record for "latest we've gone into hurricane season without a single hurricane".
 September 11 Update
 Tropical Storm Norbert continues to strengthen but remains no threat to land for now. This system is expected to keep moving west over the next few days. Norbert could get stronger this weekend and may become a hurricane. Meanwhile, the Atlantic remains quiet as we approach the peak of hurricane season.
 September 10 Update
 Tropical Storm Norbert has formed in the Eastern Pacific, with winds around 40 mph and stronger gusts. The storm is located several hundred miles south of Baja California. The forecast track keeps it moving west to west-northwest over the next few days. Some additional strengthening is possible. There are currently no coastal watches or warnings in effect.
 Meanwhile, the Atlantic remains quiet as we approach the peak of hurricane season.
 September 9 Update
 Lowell weakens to a Tropical Storm as it moves north of Hawaii. Winds are now around 65 mph, with further weakening expected over the next few days. Dangerous surf and rip currents along exposed Hawaiian beaches is expected through Thursday. As Lowell continues to pull away from Hawaii, the Atlantic remains quiet as we approach the peak of hurricane season.
 September 8 Update
 Hurricane Lowell is moving north away from the Hawaiian Islands with winds of 90 mph but is weakening. Hurricane warnings remain for Kauai and Niihau, with a tropical storm warning for Oahu. Heavy rain could cause significant flash flooding and mudslides, especially on Kauai and the Big Island.
 The Atlantic remains quiet with no tropical edvelopment expected during the next 7 days.
 September 7 Update
 The good news first: No tropical development is expected over the next 7 days in the Atlantic basin, meaning we are worry-free here in Houston for at least a week (and likely longer). While the Atlantic basin has been unusually quiet considering the time of year, the Pacific remains extremely active. Of greatest interest in Hurricane Lowell, which is rapidly approaching Hawaii and will bring flooding rains, high winds, and rough waters to the western-most Hawaiian islands tonight and tomorrow morning.
 September 6 Update
 The Atlantic Basin, which includes the Atlantic Ocean, the Gulf, and the Caribbean, remains quiet with no development expect over the next 7 days. That's great news any time of year, but especially during peak hurricane season (which it currently is). That means that here in the greater Houston area, we have no tropical troubles for at least a week. The Pacific Basin on the other hand remains very active. There are currently three named storms in the Pacific, the strongest of which is Lowell, and it should bring some indirect impacts to the western-most Hawaiian islands as it passes by the island.
 September 5 Update
 We are entering peak hurricane season, and yet no development is expected over the next 7 days in the Atlantic basin. That is great news this time of year, as the high shear brought my El Nino continues to keep things fairly quiet in the tropics. The Pacific basin is a different story, with 3 hurricanes ongoing. One of those, Lowell, is a major hurricane and could bring impacts to the western Hawaiian islands next week.
 September 4 7 a.m. Update
 Tracking 3 storms in the Pacific! Hurricane Marie is expected to continue tracking northwestward, with no direct impacts to Mexico anticipated. Farther west, Hurricane Karina is well offshore to the west of Mexico and is also expected to continue tracking northwestward. Meanwhile, Hurricane Lowell is a powerful Category 4 hurricane in the Central Pacific. Lowell will move westward before turning northward next week, and it could bring some impacts to the western Hawaiian Islands.
 September 3 7 a.m. Update
 It stays active across the Pacific, while the Atlantic is relatively quiet now that Edouard has dissipated. The remnants of Edouard are still producing heavy rain over Texas, but the National Hurricane Center has issued its final advisory on that system. In the Pacific, Hurricane Karina remains a powerful storm well offshore, while Hurricane Marie is also being monitored. And in the Central Pacific, Hurricane Lowell is a major hurricane. Swells generated by this system are spreading northward and will affect portions of the Hawaiian Islands during the next several days. These swells are likely to cause life-threatening surf and dangerous rip currents.
 September 2 7 a.m. Update
 Tropical Depression Edouard continues to weaken and the biggest threat now is heavy rain and flooding. Edouard is moving north-northwest at about 5 mph, with winds around 35 mph. The system is expected to fall apart by Wednesday night. The heaviest rain remains focused north and northeast from Houston. Total rainfall amounts between 4 to 8 inches could fall, with isolated totals up to 12 inches. That could lead to significant flash flooding, especially in low-lying and urban areas. Bottom line: Edouard is losing strength, but the flooding threat remains the main concern.
 September 1 7 p.m. Update
 After making landfall near Johnson Bayou Louisiana around 2:20 p.m., Edouard has been producing flooding rain and strong winds in the Beaumont area this afternoon. Many cars have been flooded. It's winds will slowly weaken overnight, but the heavy rain will continue. The corridor from Cleveland to Livingston will see the heaviest rain with totals of 3-6" possible. A feeder band of heavy rain is expected to develop overnight, potentially over northern Harris, Montgomery, Liberty, and Walker counties.
 September 1 10 a.m. Update
 Tropical Storm Edouard winds continue to strengthen. As of the 10 a.m. advisory, maximum sustained winds are near 50 mph with higher gusts. Additional strengthening is forecast before Edouard makes landfall today, and the storm could approach hurricane strength. Rapid weakening is expected after the center moves inland.
 September 1 7 a.m. Update
 Tropical storm Edouard continues to track west along the Gulf Coast this morning with winds of 40 mph and gusts up to 50 mph. Edouard will make landfall as a strong tropical storm with winds of 65 mph as the system is strengthening this morning with the help of minimal wind shear and shallow, very warm waters just offshore. Edouard could make landfall anywhere between High Island, TX and Cameron Parish, LA Tuesday afternoon. After that the storm will continue to move inland, bringing with it torrential tropical downpours that could lead to street and flash flooding across portions of Southeast Texas Tuesday and Wednesday.
 A Tropical Storm Warning is now in effect for Chambers and southern Liberty County. Tropical storm-force winds between 40 and 60 mph could lead to wind damage and power outages within th warned area. Coastal communities could see a potential surge between 1 to 3 feet Tuesday too.
 A Flood Watch is in effect until 7 a.m. Wednesday for Harris, Brazoria, Fort Bend, Galveston, Montgomery, Chambers, Liberty, San Jacinto and Polk counties. Heavy tropical downpours are expected that could lead to street and urban flooding as well as flash flooding at times. Around 3 to 5 inches of rain could fall widespread across the region with the Watch, though isolated totals between 6 to 9 inches of rain are possible too, especially east of I-45.
 August 31 7 p.m. Update
 Tropical Storm Edouard has officially formed in the Gulf, according to an update from the National Hurricane Center. The system is still expected to make landfall along the southeast Texas coastline on Tuesday, prompting an ABC13 Weather Alert Day for Tuesday and an ABC13 Weather Watch for Wednesday.
 August 31 1 p.m. Update
 In the latest update from the National Hurricane Center, Potential Storm Five is now Tropical Depression Five as the system now has more of a tropical structure to it. Winds as still sustained at 35 mph with gusts up to 45 mph. Tropical Depression Five is forecast to strengthen to a tropical storm later today with winds of 40 mph, which would also name it Edouard. The system is then expected to make landfall along the southeast Texas coastline somewhere between Galveston Island and the Sabine Pass Tuesday afternoon or evening as a tropical storm.
 A Flood Watch is also in effect for much of Southeast Texas as this system will bring torrential tropical downpours that could lead to street and urban flooding as well as flash flooding. Both Tuesday and Wednesday are now ABC13 Weather Watch Days because of the potential for flooding. Much of the region within the Watch will receive 3 to 5 inches of rain but some communities could see between 6 to 9 inches of rain fall within about 24 to 48 hours, hence the flood risk.
 August 31 10 a.m. Update
 Potential Storm Five has formed in the Gulf Monday morning and is expected to become tropical storm Edouard later today as the system slowly tracks west. The system as of now has 35 mph sustained winds with gusts up to 45 mph and a minimum central pressure of 1013 mb. By later Monday this system is expected to strengthen to sustained winds of 40 mph, making it a tropical storm. This system is expected to slowly track north-northwest over the next 24 hours as a tropical storm and then make landfall Tuesday afternoon somewhere between Galveston and Sabine Pass. A Tropical Storm Warning is now in effect for Chambers County as tropical storm force winds, and elevated storm surge of 1 to 2 feet and heavy rainfall is expected Tuesday.
 August 31 7 a.m. Update
 A small area of low pressure in the northern Gulf is producing showers and thunderstorms about 100 miles south of Louisiana. It could strengthen into a short-lived tropical depression or tropical storm before reaching the Upper Texas or southwest Louisiana coast tonight or early Tuesday. Heavy rain is the main concern, with tropical storm watches or warnings possible later today. A Hurricane Hunter will investigate the system this morning to give forecasters a better idea of its strength and track. The chance of development is 70 percent.
 Meanwhile, the remnants of Tropical Storm Dolly are producing storms near the Caribbean. Strong upper-level winds should limit development over the next couple of days, but heavy rain and gusty winds are possible across Puerto Rico, the Virgin Islands and nearby islands.
 August 30 2 p.m. Update
 The disturbance in the northern Gulf now has a 50% chance of forming into a tropical system within the next two days as it slowly jogs west. The region of swirling showers and storms is in a region that would favor potential tropical development over the next 24 to 48 hours. Regardless of that, heavy rain will be the main concern for Southeast Texas as this wave will reach the Texas coastline Tuesday with showers and storms possible through Wednesday. At this time the main risk would be the possibility for flooding or even flash flooding if conditions are right.
 August 30 Update
 The NHC has increased development odds to 30% on a disturbance in the northern Gulf. The eventual path and timing of the disturbance are fairly well set, it should move into Southeast Texas on Tuesday (afternoon or evening). The question that remains is whether or not this disturbance is able to become better organized and strengthen before it arrives. Some forecast models do show a tighter low pressure, capable of bringing a tropical depression or tropical storm into Southeast Texas. However most forecast models keep it as a disorganized and beneficial rainfall maker. For now we have rain chances on Tuesday set for 60%.
 August 29 Update
 The National Hurricane Center has tagged a disturbance in the Eastern Gulf with a 10% chance of potential development. While our overall level of concern is fairly low, we do expect it will gradually slide west, increasing moisture in our neck of the woods and bringing back more legitimate rain chances by Tuesday.
 Elsewhere, the remnants of Tropical Storm Dolly continue towards the Caribbean. Again, development odds are low, but it's worth keeping an eye on over the next few days.
 August 28 11 AM Update
 Dolly has weakened into an open tropical wave. The remnants are moving west at about 25 mph and could reach the Leeward Islands Saturday night into Sunday. Winds are still near 40 mph, but they're expected to weaken below tropical-storm strength Saturday. Heavy rain could impact the Leeward Islands, with rain spreading to the Virgin Islands, Puerto Rico and Hispaniola Sunday into Monday. Flash flooding is possible.
 August 28 7:30 AM Update
 Tropical Storm Dolly is moving quickly west at about 24 mph. It could approach the Leeward Islands this weekend, but Dolly is expected to weaken into a tropical wave before reaching the islands. Dolly has maximum winds of 40 mph, with stronger gusts. Heavy rain could reach the Leeward Islands late Saturday into Sunday, with rain spreading toward the Virgin Islands, Puerto Rico and Hispaniola Sunday and Monday. Flash flooding is possible.
 August 27 10:30 AM Update
 Tropical Storm Dolly has formed over the central Atlantic, about east of the Leeward Islands. Dolly has winds of around 40 mph and is moving west at about 24 mph. Dolly is expected to approach the Caribbean islands this weekend, although the latest forecast has it weakening into a tropical wave before reaching land. Heavy rain could begin affecting the Leeward Islands late Saturday into Sunday, followed by the Virgin Islands, Puerto Rico and Hispaniola Sunday into Monday. The rain could lead to flash flooding, especially in mountainous areas.
 August 27 7 AM Update
 A tropical wave southwest of the Cabo Verde Islands has become better organized, with stronger showers and thunderstorms. If it continues to strengthen, it could become a tropical depression or tropical storm later today. However, conditions are expected to become less favorable starting Friday, which could stop further development. Formation odds have increased to 90% over the next 48 hours.
 August 26 Update
 A tropical wave several hundred miles southwest of the Cabo Verde Islands is producing showers and thunderstorms. Conditions are favorable enough for it to become a tropical depression within the next day or two. It is expected to move west to west-northwest across the central Atlantic. The chance of development is 60% over the next 48 hours. There is no immediate threat to the U.S. at this time.
 August 25 Update
 There are two areas with tropical development potential over the next 7 days. A low near Bermuda is moving north. It could briefly become a tropical depression or storm today, but unfavorable conditions should limit development by tonight or Wednesday. Meanwhile, in the eastern Atlantic, a low south-southeast of the Cabo Verde Islands has a better chance of developing as it moves west across the Atlantic. Formation odds have increased to 70%. This system could become a tropical depression over the next few days as it moves west to west-northwest across the Atlantic. However, conditions may become less favorable for development by the weekend.
 August 24 Update
 A tropical wave that is just now rolling off the coast of Africa is worth keeping an eye on. Right now the NHC has placed development odds at 60% on this budding system, but most forecast models are fairly confident it will become our next named storm. The good news here is that earlier and stronger development also likely means an earlier turn to the north, and the overwhelmingly likely outcome is a storm that turns north long before it ever reaches the US. We'll keep watching it, but the concern level here is low.
 Another system is gradually lifting north as it parallels the eastern seaboard, impacts here in Texas are zero, and impacts to the US in general are minimal.
 August 23 Update
 There are 3 areas that are currently tagged for potential development in the Atlantic Basin, but only one of those has even the potential to impact the US. A tropical wave in the open Atlantic is now tagged with a 50% chance of development as it moves west across the Atlantic. While it's still a long way away, forecast models have been fairly aggressive in developing this potential storm. The likely outcome is an eventual named system which curves north before ever reaching the US, but we have plenty of time to keep an eye on it. I'm also seeing a few models trying to pop a storm in the Gulf in the first week of September, that's far from a lock, but is something we will be watching closely as we enter the peak of hurricane season.
 August 22 Update
 Tropical activity has increased over the Atlantic as we monitor three tropical waves for development. A strong area of low pressure is several hundred miles west of Portugal. It could briefly take on some tropical or subtropical characteristics today or Sunday as it moves toward Portugal and northwestern Spain. Formation odds at 20 percent through the next 7 days. In the Central Atlantic, some disorganized showers near Bermuda has a low chance for development, 20 percent. Finally, a tropical wave is expected to move off the coast of Africa early next week. Development will be slow to occur as this system tracks west toward the Caribbean. Formation odds at 30%.
 Meanwhile in the Pacific, the Hawaiian islands preparing for another tropical storm to bring heavy rain and gusty winds. Tropical Storm Moke is forecast to gradually strengthen during the next day or two, followed by a steady weakening trend as the storm passes well south of the smaller main Hawaiian Islands early next week.
 August 21 Update
 Tropical Depresstion Two has formed in the central Pacific and is forecast to become Moke over the next 24 hours. Heavy rain and large waves is expected to impact parts of the Hawaiian islands for a second weekend in a row as the center of the system passes south of the Big Island of Hawaii and then the smaller main Hawaiian Islands by early next week. Lala remains a hurricane as it moves deeper into the central Pacific.
 A couple of areas are being monitored in the Atlantic, but neither is a threat to the Gulf. One low-pressure system north of the Azores could briefly take on some tropical or subtropical characteristics this weekend as it moves toward Portugal and Spain. The chance of development is low, around 20%. Another weak low east-southeast of Bermuda is producing some disorganized showers and storms. Any development is expected to be slow, and the system will drift west before turning north early next week.
 August 20 Update
 Lala remains a strong hurricane as it nears the northwestern Hawaiian Islands. Tropical and hurricane warnings remain in effect. Showers and thunderstorms are getting better organized around a low-pressure system well east-southeast of Hawaii. Conditions are favorable for this system to strengthen, and a tropical depression could form as soon as tonight or Thursday.
 Meanwhile in the Atlantic, we are watching some tropical waves and Saharan dust emerging from Africa. Tropical development is not expected over the next 7 days.
 August 19 Update
 Lala becomes a category 4 hurricane and expected to impact the northwestern Hawaiian islands. Tropical storm and hurricane warnings have been issued as large waves will begin to develop. Meanwhile in the Atlantic, we are watching some tropical waves and Saharan dust emerging from Africa. Tropical development is not expected over the next 7 days.
 August 18 Update
 Lala has restrengthened to a hurricane as it moves farther away from Hawaii. Lala is expected to remain a hurricane for the next several days as it remains over the central Pacific. Meanwhile in the Atlantic, we are watching some tropical waves and Saharan dust emerging from Africa. No tropical development is expected over the next 7 days.
 August 17 Update
 Tropical Storm Lala continues to weaken as it pulls away from the Hawaiian islands. Potential for heavy rain and isolated flooding concerns continue through Monday before tapering off. Meanwhile in the Atlantic, no tropical development is expected over the next 7 days.
 August 16 Update
 Hurricane Lala retains its strength this morning as a category 1 storm as it passes by the Hawaiian Islands. The storm will continue to bring storm force winds and torrential, flooding rains to the islands as it passes by, though will move away from the state late Sunday. There are also two other areas to monitor for potential tropical development in the Pacific. Meanwhile in the Atlantic, no tropical development is expected over the next 7 days.
 August 15 PM Update
 Lala has become a Hurricane off the coast of Hawaii. The center is expected to pass just south of the island but the dirty side of the storm will spread heavy, flooding rains, a 103' storm surge, and 70+ mph winds onshore through the weekend. Development odds in the Atlantic have dropped to zero.
 August 15 Update
 The tropical wave that passed by the Windward Islands Friday now has a 0% chance of forming into a tropical system in the southern Caribbean. This is due to unfavorable conditions with wind shear play a big role in that. It's also why there's now only a 20% chance for the tropical wave in the central Atlantic to develop too. As this wave approaches the Caribbean next week, it'll also run into a region of wind shear that would make it difficult for a tropical system to form.
 Meanwhile in the Pacific, Tropical Storm Lala will pass by Hawaii Saturday and could bring hurricane force winds and flooding to the Big Island.
 August 14 6 a.m. Update
 Two named storms in the Pacific, but only one could bring hurricane conditions to Hawaii this weekend. Tropical Storm Lala forecast to become a hurricane as it approaches the big island of Hawaii by Saturday. Hurricane conditions are expected on the Big Island of Hawaii by early Saturday, with tropical storm conditions possible in Maui County by late Saturday. Rainfall totals of 8 to 12 inches across Maui and the Big Island with maximum totals of 25 inches possible across the Big Island.
 Meanwhile in the Atlantic, there are two tropical waves to watch. A tropical wave about 650 miles east of the Lesser Antilles is becoming less organized. Stronger winds higher in the atmosphere and dry air are making development less likely. Another tropical wave, southwest of the Cabo Verde Islands, is producing disorganized showers and thunderstorms. Conditions are favorable for gradual development, and this system could become a tropical depression during the next 7 days. Formation odds around 50%.
 August 13 11 a.m. Update
 Cristobal dissipates over the northern Atlantic. The National Hurricane Center has issued its final advisory.
 August 13 7 a.m. Update
 Cristobal weakens to a Tropical Depression and is expected to dissipate. We are also monitoring the deep tropics as tropical activity begins to ramp up. One wave has a high chance of becoming the next named storm, Dolly, as it approaches the Windward Islands this weekend. We have plenty of time to monitor it, and there is no threat to the Gulf or Houston at this time.
 August 12 10 a.m. Update
 We now have Tropical Storm Cristobal in the North Atlantic with winds of 45 mph and gusts up to 60 mph. This will be a short-lived tropical storm as it speeds across the North Atlantic at 25 mph, likely dissipating tomorrow. Meanwhile, we're keeping a close eye on the deep tropics with the tropical wave train getting going. One wave has a high likelihood of becoming the next named storm, Dolly, as it approaches the Windward Islands this weekend. We've got plenty of time to watch it, though it poses no threat to the Gulf or Houston at this time.
 August 12 Update
 There are three areas of potential development in the Atlantic with one that has a high likelihood of becoming the next named storm of the season. This tropical wave in the central Atlantic is now invest 92L, and as of Wednesday morning the swirling area of showers and storms is looking more like a tropical system and could become a tropical depression heading into the weekend. Current spaghetti model plots send this potential storm into the Caribbean next week, though some have it still hugging the eastern Caribbean in the Atlantic Ocean. At this time this tropical wave does not pose a threat to the gulf or Houston, and we have plenty of time to watch it.
 Behind this wave in the deep tropics there another wave of showers and storms near the Cabo Verde Islands that has a low chance of developing. Then the tropical wave in the north Atlantic now has 50/50 odds of becoming a tropical system too.
 August 11 Update
 We're continuing to monitor three areas of potential development in the Atlantic. One in the northern Atlantic has low odds of developing as well as the wave closest to the Caribbean in the deep tropics. The one wave to monitor that could become a tropical storm is in the central Atlantic. A region of low pressure and thunderstorm activity currently 500 miles to the southwest of the Cabo Verde Islands will be moving into a region that will favor potential tropical development. That wave now has a 70% chance of developing into a tropical system over the next 7 days.
 Then in the Pacific there are two areas of shower and storm activity that have medium to high odds of forming over the next 7 days.
 August 10 Update
 The Atlantic basin has come alive with three areas to monitor for tropical development over the next 7 days. The Atlantic has come alive this week. Three waves to watch: A tropical wave midway between Africa and the Lesser Antilles has a 10% chance of development over the next 7 days as it moves west. Disorganized showers and storms south of the Cabo Verde Islands could become more organized later this week. 60% chance of development over 7 days. This is the area we're watching most closely. A weak system near Bermuda has just a 10% chance of development before cooler water shuts it down later this week. No immediate tropical threats to land, but the eastern Atlantic bears watching later this week.
 August 9 Update
 As expected this time of year, things are getting a bit more active in the Atlantic! We now have two areas of potential development being monitored by the National Hurricane Center, one with 20% development odds, then a follow-up wave behind it at 40% odds. A few bits of good news here: First, these waves are still way out in the Atlantic, closer to Africa than the Caribbean, so we have plenty of time to keep an eye on them. Second, most long-range forecast models either curve a storm north well ahead of reaching the US, or it brings a storm into the Caribbean, where high wind shear brings an unfavorable storm environment, and leads to a storm that quickly decays before making it into the Gulf. We'll keep a close on eye things as always, but the overall concern level here is low.
 August 8 Update
 After a quiet stretch in the tropics following Bertha, we have a new area of potential development to monitor off the coast of Africa. The National Hurricane Center is currently putting 20% development odds on the system, which is one of many tropical waves in the area. The good news for us is that high wind shear in the Caribbean will make any development closer to home very difficult, and it's unlikely this system ever makes it into the Gulf.
 August 7 Update
 NOAA is doubling down on a "quieter than average season", updating the official hurricane forecast with even lower numbers than the initial forecast in May. A record-breaking El Nino is the main reason for the updated forecast, with El Nino years bringing an increase in wind shear to the Gulf and Caribbean, and lessening storm development odds. No tropical development is expected over the next 7 days.
 August 6 12 p.m. Update
 NOAA released their August update to the 2026 hurricane outlook, and they have dropped the total number of named storms and major hurricanes expected by one storm each. The primary driver in this year's hurricane season is a rapidly strengthening El Nino in the Pacific, which tends to bring high wind shear over the Atlantic that cuts down on the number and strength of storms. Watch the video update for a more in-depth look from Chief Meteorologist Travis Herzog on how this El Nino will impact the hurricane season ahead with specific implications for Texas.

 August 6 Update
 While the Atlantic remains quiet, the Pacific is turning more active. A tropical wave in the eastern Pacific is only producing a few showers and thunderstorms, but it's moving into a much drier environment, so tropical development is low at 20 percent.
 Another disturbance in the Pacific has a 30 percent chance of forming into a tropical depression as it tracks west at 10 to 15 mph. At this point, neither of these disturbances will be a threat to land.
 August 5 Update
 The Atlantic basin remains quiet as Saharan dust and strong wind shear keeps atmospheric conditions unfavorable for tropical development over the next 7 days.
 In the Pacific, we are monitoring two tropical waves for tropical development. One wave is producing showers and thunderstorms, but development remains unlikely. Chance of development: 20% over the next 7 days.
 A second tropical wave is expected to move into a slightly more favorable environment this weekend. Formation odds are also near 20%. No immediate tropical concerns with either of the waves.
 August 4 Update
 A widespread plume of Saharan dust remains stretched across much of the tropical Atlantic, helping keep tropical activity at a minimum. The dry, dusty air limits thunderstorm development and makes it harder for tropical systems to strengthen. No areas of concern are expected over the next seven days.
 August 3 Update
 A large plume of Saharan dust continues to blanket much of the tropical Atlantic, helping keep the basin quiet with no immediate areas of concern for tropical development. The dry, dusty air suppresses thunderstorms and makes it more difficult for tropical systems to organize. While we're entering the heart of hurricane season, conditions remain unfavorable for development over the next 7 days.
 August 2 Update
 August is typically when the tropics start coming to life in the Atlantic Basin, but so far, so good. No tropical development is expected over the next 7 days, partly due to a wide swath of Saharan dust blanketing much of the Caribbean and main development zone of the Atlantic.
 August 1 Update
 All quiet in the Atlantic Basin as we kick off August. No development is expected over the next 7 days. Now is the time to remain vigilant, as tropical activity typically ramps up dramatically later this month.
 July 31 Update
 The Atlantic basin remains quiet as Saharan dust and strong wind shear keeps atmospheric conditions unfavorable for tropical development.
 In the eastern Pacific, Genevieve is now a tropical storm and is located southwest of Mexico. Dangerous rip currents will continue along the west coast of Mexico and Southern California. Gradual weakening is forecast during the next few days, and Genevieve is expected to become a remnant low over the weekend.
 July 30 Update
 Fausto has dissipated. Meanwhile, Genevieve is a Category 1 hurricane. It will generate large swells along the beaches of Southern California this week, but is not expected to directly impact land
